summary.text: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars whose orbit lies in a plane along our line of sight, so the stars eclipse and transit each other.
Because the stars pass in front of one another, the pair changes in brightness, and that change is how such a pair is detected.
Eclipsing binaries belong to the photometric binaries, and a pair can fit several observing classes at once.

facts.label: Orbit alignment
facts.value: Orbit plane lies along our line of sight

facts.label: How detected
facts.value: By changes in brightness caused by an eclipse

facts.label: Wider group
facts.value: Photometric binaries, with other brightness-changing binaries

facts.label: Class overlap
facts.value: Several spectroscopic binaries are also eclipsing

items.prompt: Two stars orbit each other in a plane that runs straight along our line of sight. What will we see over each orbit?

options.label: The two stars stay side by side, never overlapping
Each star passes across the other
Both stars vanish for good after the first pass
The two stars spiral into one another

items.explain: When a binary orbits in a plane along our line of sight, its components eclipse and transit each other.

items.prompt: Using only measurements of how much light arrives over time, what pattern points to an eclipsing binary?

options.label: Brightness dips as one star passes in front of the other
A single star's position drifting as an unseen partner tugs it
Two separate points of light visible through a telescope
A steady brightness that never changes at all

items.explain: Eclipsing binaries are detected photometrically, by changes in brightness caused by an eclipse.

items.prompt: A pair of stars is known to be an eclipsing binary. Can it also be classified another way?

options.label: No, every binary belongs to just one class
No, an eclipse rules out every other method
Yes, some are also spectroscopic binaries
Yes, but only if the two stars match in brightness

items.explain: Any binary star can belong to several classes; several spectroscopic binaries are also eclipsing binaries.

items.prompt: Eclipsing binaries are grouped with other binaries that change brightness as they orbit. What is that wider group called?

options.label: Photometric binaries
Visual binaries
Spectroscopic binaries
Astrometric binaries

items.explain: Eclipsing binaries, together with other binaries that change brightness as they orbit, are photometric binaries.

items.prompt: No one can put a lone star on a scale. What do binary stars like these let astronomers do?

options.label: Count the planets around each star
Photograph the surface of each star
Predict the exact date each star will die
Measure stellar masses directly

items.explain: Binary stars allow direct measurement of stellar masses and test theories of stellar evolution.

items.prompt: A telescope can split many binaries into two separate stars. How is an eclipsing binary found instead?

options.label: By splitting the pair with a more powerful telescope
By brightness changes from an eclipse, not by seeing two stars
By measuring how far one star strays from a straight path
By detecting radio pulses coming from the pair

items.explain: Visual binaries are resolved by observation, while eclipsing binaries are found photometrically through brightness changes caused by an eclipse.
